terms.gloss: in proportion, proportionally; with a genitive, in proportion to
terms.grammar: phrase: prō with the ablative of portiō
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.320: prō portiōne rērum
Cato Agr. 106: prō portiōne ea omnia facitō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical phrase; portiō alone, “a share”, is post-Augustan (Lewis & Short). For “a large proportion of” Latin says magna pars (see most, the greater part).

terms.gloss: proportionately, each by its due share
terms.grammar: phrase: prō with the ablative of rata pars, a fixed share
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.94: perinde ut cuique data sunt prō ratā parte
Cic. Rep. 2.67: utinam ex omnī senātū prō ratā parte esset!
terms.comment: Rata pars is a fixed, reckoned share (ratus, from reor); the phrase is the source of English “pro rata”.

evidence: Varr. L.L. 10.2: prōportiō, quod dīcunt ἀνάλογον (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A learned word of grammar and mathematics, which Cicero offers as a new coinage for Greek analogia (Lewis & Short); in talk the phrase prō portiōne is more natural.

phrases.latin: oportet, ut aedibus ac templīs vestibula et aditūs, sīc causīs prīncipia prō portiōne rērum praepōnere
phrases.english: as houses and temples have forecourts and entrances, so cases should be given openings in proportion to their matter

phrases.latin: Omnia ista, perinde ut cuique data sunt prō ratā parte, ita aut longa aut brevia dīcuntur.
phrases.english: All those things are called long or short according to the share each has been given.

sources: Lewis & Short: portio · Lewis & Short: ratus · Lewis & Short: proportio

Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j).
